name: Leg curl
angleNote: Knee flexion: 0° = leg straight (start), 120° = heel towards the buttocks. Hip at the origin.

segments.massNote: Segment mass as a fraction of body mass, and centre of mass as a fraction of the segment length from its proximal end, from de Leva's adjusted Zatsiorsky-Seluyanov table (young adult males). The lower leg includes the foot (combined centre of mass along knee → ankle; the foot's own position is approximated).
segments.massSource: de Leva P (1996). Adjustments to Zatsiorsky-Seluyanov's segment inertia parameters. J Biomech 29(9):1223–1230. doi:10.1016/0021-9290(95)00178-6 (Table 4, males)
segments.note: Hip→knee and knee→ankle in metres, typical adult.

strengthCurve.label: Knee flexor strength
strengthCurve.note: Relative isometric knee-flexion torque vs knee flexion, peak about 30°, measured seated with the hip flexed about 70° (tested 0–103°). Relative curve = cos(C2·(θ − C3)) with the 18–25-year-old male means of Table 3; points only inside the tested range, so the app holds the end values flat beyond it. Peak torque default from the same table's C1 (young men, scaled to 73 kg and 1.75 m). The seated test position matches the seated leg curl best; lying, the hamstrings are shorter and somewhat weaker (not modelled). Variants correct this for the hip angle (two-joint hamstrings): see each variant's strength note.
strengthCurve.source: Anderson DE, Madigan ML, Nussbaum MA (2007). Maximum voluntary joint torque as a function of joint angle and angular velocity: model development and application to the lower limb. J Biomech 40(14):3105–3113. doi:10.1016/j.jbiomech.2007.03.022

muscles.regionSharesNote: How the hamstrings' activity splits between the heads (close-up only): MRI signal rise after the Nordic hamstring exercise, eccentric knee flexion with the hips straight (6 women): semitendinosus 58.0%, semimembranosus 33.3%, biceps femoris 25.4% (long head) and 22.5% (short head; drawn together, averaged), as fractions of the most active head (Table). Applied to both leg curls; the seated curl's bent hip wasn't tested. Surface EMG in maximal knee flexion found the inner and outer hamstrings about equally active (Park & Lim: 57–62% of maximum), so the semitendinosus' lead is method-dependent.
muscles.regionSharesSource: Messer DJ, Bourne MN, Williams MD, Al Najjar A, Shield AJ (2018). Hamstring muscle use in women during hip extension and the Nordic hamstring exercise: a functional magnetic resonance imaging study. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 48(8):607–612. doi:10.2519/jospt.2018.7748; Park S, Lim W (2023). Comparison of muscle activity of hamstrings as knee flexors and hip extensors and effect of tibial and hip rotation on the contribution of hamstrings. J Bodyw Mov Ther 34:1–5. doi:10.1016/j.jbmt.2023.04.029
muscles.name: Hamstrings
muscles.note: Cross the hip as well; their length (and strength) depends on hip angle, which these weights ignore. The leg curl favours the medial hamstrings over the biceps femoris (the lowest lateral-to-medial ratio of 10 exercises, Bourne et al.).
muscles.source: Bourne MN, Williams MD, Opar DA, Al Najjar A, Kerr GK, Shield AJ (2017). Impact of exercise selection on hamstring muscle activation. Br J Sports Med 51(13):1021–1028. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2015-095739 (24 men, 10 exercises)

muscles.name: Gastrocnemius
muscles.note: Calf muscle that also crosses the knee and helps flex it. Pointing the toes shortens it: its EMG was 44% higher toes pointed than pulled up with the knee straight (Marchetti et al., lying), while knee-flexion force was lower; the weight doesn't follow the foot setting.
muscles.source: TODO: check against EMG literature; Marchetti PH, Magalhaes RA, Gomes WA, da Silva JJ, Stecyk SD, Whiting WC (2021). Different knee and ankle positions affect force and muscle activation during prone leg curl in trained subjects. J Strength Cond Res 35(12):3322–3326. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000003333 (Results and Table 1: 15 resistance-trained men, isometric, prone, hip at 15°)

phases.name: Mid-range
phases.text: Lying or standing with an ankle weight, the lower leg passes horizontal near 90°, where gravity's torque peaks.

phases.name: Fully bent
phases.text: Heel near the buttocks; hamstrings are weakest here.

variants.name: Lying leg curl machine

camProfiles.label: Rising cam (most commercial machines)
camProfiles.note: Effective radius in metres: joint torque per unit of stack weight. An estimate: one patent's survey of several commercial leg machines found cam radii of 6 inches with the leg straight rising to 12 inches at the end of the curl (Cunningham), and a 1983 check of a Nautilus leg curl found the resistance rising through most of the movement (Harman). Here: doubling from straight to fully bent, linear in between (the in-between shape isn't known), 0.30 m at the top, nominal. The knee flexors are strongest near straight, so this shape fights the strength curve; a 1992 study of the Nautilus leg curl found the same mismatch (Pizzimenti, abstract only).
camProfiles.source: Cunningham TJ (2010). Exercise apparatus. US Patent 7,744,507 B2 (filed 2007; background: cam radii observed on several commercial leg machines); Harman E (1983). Resistive torque analysis of 5 Nautilus exercise machines. Med Sci Sports Exerc 15(2):113. doi:10.1249/00005768-198315020-00117 (conference abstract; cam radii from photographs); Pizzimenti MA (1992). Mechanical analysis of the Nautilus leg curl machine. Can J Sport Sci 17(1):41–48 (abstract)

camProfiles.label: Peak mid-range (illustrative)
camProfiles.note: Effective radius in metres: joint torque per unit of stack weight, including any lever or pulley ratio. Illustrative shape, not measured from a specific machine.

camProfiles.label: Round pulley (constant)
camProfiles.note: A plain round pulley: the lever between the belt and the axle never changes, so the resistance torque is the same at every angle (physics, no source needed). Many plate-loaded and budget machines work like this. Radius 0.30 m, nominal (stack kg don't compare between machines).
camProfiles.source: Physics: a round pulley's radius is constant (no source needed)

variants.notes: Face down with the hip straight. The pad is behind the ankle; lifting the lower leg's weight also adds torque until it passes vertical (90°).

strengthScale.note: hip straight, so the hamstrings are shorter: knee-flexion strength about 61% of the seated test's. Guex et al. measured 62 Nm with the hip straight vs 110 Nm at 90° of hip flexion (knee at 45°); the base curve was measured with the hip at about 70° (101 Nm by interpolation). Measured at one knee angle only, so the factor is applied across the range. Black et al. found the same: 48 Nm lying on the back (hip at about 10°) vs 78 Nm sitting (hip at about 80°), a ratio of 0.62; Worrell et al. also found the hamstrings weaker supine. Check of the curve's shape lying: Marchetti et al. measured the force with the knee at 90° at 0.66–0.68 of the straight-knee force (hip at 15°); the base curve gives 0.61 ÷ 0.90 = 0.68.
strengthScale.source: Guex K, Gojanovic B, Millet GP (2012). Influence of hip-flexion angle on hamstrings isokinetic activity in sprinters. J Athl Train 47(4):390–395. doi:10.4085/1062-6050-47.4.04 (Table: isometric, knee at 45°, 10 sprinters); Black SJ, Woodhouse ML, Suttmiller S, Shall L (1993). Influence of hip position on electromyographic and torque productions in the knee. J Sport Rehabil 2(1):26–34. doi:10.1123/jsr.2.1.26 (Table 1: 24 recreational athletes, isokinetic 30°/s); Worrell TW, Perrin DH, Denegar CR (1989). The influence of hip position on quadriceps and hamstring peak torque and reciprocal muscle group ratio values. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 11(3):104–107; Marchetti PH, Magalhaes RA, Gomes WA, da Silva JJ, Stecyk SD, Whiting WC (2021). Different knee and ankle positions affect force and muscle activation during prone leg curl in trained subjects. J Strength Cond Res 35(12):3322–3326. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000003333 (Results and Table 1: 15 resistance-trained men, isometric, prone, hip at 15°)

variants.notes: Hip bent 90°, so the hamstrings work from a longer length. Here the lower leg's weight helps the curl. The extra strength from the longer hamstrings is not modelled.

strengthScale.note: hip bent 90°, hamstrings lengthened: about 109% of the base curve's strength (Guex et al.: 110 Nm at 90° of hip flexion vs about 101 Nm at the base curve's 70°). Measured at one knee angle only.
strengthScale.source: Guex K, Gojanovic B, Millet GP (2012). Influence of hip-flexion angle on hamstrings isokinetic activity in sprinters. J Athl Train 47(4):390–395. doi:10.4085/1062-6050-47.4.04 (Table: isometric, knee at 45°, 10 sprinters)

variants.name: Standing leg curl (ankle weight)
variants.notes: Torque = (m·L + lower-leg weight)·g·sin(knee angle): nothing at the start, largest with the lower leg horizontal at 90°.

wger.name: Leg Curls (laying)
wger.note: Checked against wger's public exercise list (id = the number in the page address). This is the lying leg curl, the exercise's default variant.

placementStrength.note: Knee-flexion strength with the toes pulled up (ankle dorsiflexed) vs pointed (plantarflexed): 1.10 ± 0.11 times as strong seated and 1.11 ± 0.08 lying, at 60°/s (13 men; 1.14 seated at 180°/s). The gastrocnemius, which crosses the knee too, is longer with the toes up. The base curve's ankle position isn't reported, so 'relaxed' is taken as halfway: toes up × 1.05, pointed × 0.95. Measured isokinetically, applied at every knee angle. The same dataset has lying at 0.70 of seated (this app: 0.61 ÷ 1.09 = 0.56, from Guex et al.). Marchetti et al. found more (isometric, lying, toes pulled up as far as possible vs pointed): 22% stronger with the knee at 90° (significant) and 17% with it straight (not significant); biceps femoris EMG didn't change. The app keeps Vuk's 10%, measured through the whole range.
placementStrength.source: Vuk S (2023). Active Insufficiency [dataset]. Mendeley Data, v1. doi:10.17632/jyp4jg3zxm.1 (CC BY 4.0; sheet PT: isokinetic knee-flexion peak torque, 13 physically active men, seated and lying, ankle dorsiflexed vs plantarflexed); Marchetti PH, Magalhaes RA, Gomes WA, da Silva JJ, Stecyk SD, Whiting WC (2021). Different knee and ankle positions affect force and muscle activation during prone leg curl in trained subjects. J Strength Cond Res 35(12):3322–3326. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000003333 (Results and Table 1: 15 resistance-trained men, isometric, prone, hip at 15°)

placement.label: Foot
placement.hint: Pulling the toes up stretches the calf muscle (gastrocnemius), which also bends the knee: in 13 men knee flexion was about 10% stronger with the toes up than pointed, seated and lying alike (Vuk 2023); in a lying isometric test 17–22% (Marchetti et al.). Hamstring EMG didn't change. The torque the load makes is the same; only the strength changes.
